summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe permanent wave (perm): consult with the client and analyse her hair and scalp, do the skin, strand and test-curl checks, choose the lotion and rods, section and wind the hair, process it with test curls, rinse and neutralise, and give aftercare. It also covers the curl reformation (soft curl) for very curly natural hair, the faults to avoid, and clean-up and records.

blocks.p: This unit covers the whole permanent wave service, from the moment you greet the client to the moment you write the result on her record card. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees. A perm changes the shape of the hair with chemicals, so it is one of the services where a mistake does the most harm: broken hair, a burnt scalp or a curl that drops in a week. Careful checks before you start matter more than speed.

A perm is a **chemical service in two steps**. The waving lotion softens the hair so that it can take the shape of the rod. The neutraliser fixes the new shape. Everything else in this unit, from the tests to the timing, exists to make those two steps safe and even.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's salon: a water wrap of a basic and a bricklay wrap on practice heads, and a full perm service on a model or a human-hair practice head. The assessor watches your consultation, safety, wrapping, timing, test curls, clean-up and records, not only the finished curl.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hair, the rods and the work area. Never photograph a client's or model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Waving lotion and neutraliser can irritate the skin, burn the scalp, sting the eyes and give off strong fumes. The hazards are well known, and every one of them can be prevented.

blocks.h: Hazards and how you prevent them

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Lotion or neutraliser on your skin
Dermatitis (red, itchy, cracked skin); allergy that can last for life
Wear gloves for the whole service: wrapping, applying, rinsing and neutralising
Wear an apron
Dry your hands and use hand cream; report sore skin early
Lotion on the client's skin
Irritation, burns, blisters
Barrier cream round the hairline, ears and nape
A strip of cotton wool (or a neck strip) round the hairline, changed when it is wet
Apply lotion carefully to the rods, not to the skin
Lotion or neutraliser in the eyes
Pain, burns, damage to sight
Keep a towel round the client's neck and a dry towel in her hand to dab the face
Never lean the client back over the basin with lotion in her hair
Know where the eyewash and the clean water are
Strong fumes
Headache, sore throat, breathing trouble, feeling sick
Work in a well-ventilated room
Keep lids on bottles and bowls
Offer fresh air to a client who feels unwell
Wrong chemical mixes
Heat, fumes, spoilt hair
Use the lotion and neutraliser from the same maker
Never mix products from different makers
Never mix perm products with bleach or other cleaning chemicals
Metal tools and bowls
The metal can react with the chemicals and spoil the result
Use plastic or glass bowls, plastic clips and combs
Use plastic or rubber-coated clips; keep metal away from lotion on the hair
Spills and wet floors
Slips and falls; spoilt clothes
Wipe up at once
Put out a wet floor sign until it is dry

blocks.note: If waving lotion or neutraliser gets into the client's eye, rinse the eye **at once** with plenty of clean, cool running water, tilting her head so the water runs away from the other eye. Keep rinsing for at least 10 to 15 minutes, do not let her rub it, and get medical help. Tell your instructor and write it in the accident book. If lotion burns the skin, rinse the area with plenty of cool water and get help.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: If the client says her scalp is burning, itching or stinging during processing, **stop**. Rinse the lotion off the area at once with lukewarm water, tell the instructor, and do not carry on. Never tell a client that burning is normal.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Keep lotions and neutralisers in their own labelled containers, closed tight, in a **cool, dry place out of direct sunlight**. Jamaica's heat spoils the strength of perm products and can make bottles swell or leak.
Never pour products into unlabelled bottles, and never keep them in food or drink bottles.
Use the oldest stock first and check the date and the open-jar symbol on the label.
Read the label and the maker's instructions before every perm. For chemicals, read the safety data sheet, which gives hazards and first-aid steps.
Mix or measure only what you need. **Never put used or left-over lotion back into the bottle.** Throw it away as the maker and the Centre say.
Keep drinks and food away from the work area.

blocks.note: Wear gloves and wash your hands before and after every client. Keep your nails short and smooth, so that you do not scratch the client's scalp or tear your gloves.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V (220 V for some heavy equipment) at 50 Hz. Hood dryers and heat caps used for acid perms must have undamaged cables and plugs, and must never be used with wet hands or near spilt water.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: The bonds that hold the hair's shape

blocks.p: Most of a hair is the **cortex**, made of long fibres of a protein called **keratin**. The fibres are held together by cross-links called **bonds**. Three kinds matter to you.

head: Bond
How strong
What breaks it
Why it matters
rows: Hydrogen bonds
Weak, but there are very many
Water and heat; they re-form as the hair dries and cools
They give a temporary set (wet set, blow-dry). A shampoo undoes it.
Salt bonds
Weak
Changes in pH (acid or alkali)
They also break and re-form easily, so they do not hold a perm.
Disulphide bonds
Strong
Only by chemicals (waving lotion, relaxer)
They decide the shape of the hair: straight, wavy or curly. A perm changes them, so the new shape is lasting.

blocks.h: What the perm does, in two steps

flow: Hair is wound on rods of the size you chose
Waving lotion swells the hair and breaks some disulphide bonds (reduction)
The hair softens and takes the shape of the rod
The lotion is rinsed out when the test curl is right
Neutraliser re-forms the bonds in the new shape (oxidation)
The curl is now fixed and lasts until the hair grows out or is cut

ul: **Reduction** is the chemical change that breaks the bonds. The waving lotion is a **reducing agent**.
**Oxidation** is the chemical change that re-forms them. The neutraliser is an **oxidising agent**, most often **hydrogen peroxide** (some makers use a bromate).
A perm changes only the hair that was wound. New growth comes in with the natural shape, so a perm needs redoing on the new growth, or the client lives with the two textures as it grows out.
Do **not** call a perm 'permanent' in the sense that it cannot be damaged: it changes the hair's structure, and the hair is always weaker afterwards.

blocks.note: The lotion needs time, the right strength and the right rod. If it works too little, the curl is weak and falls out. If it works too much, the hair is over-processed: weak, frizzy and hard to comb. Your job is to stop at exactly the right point, and test curls tell you when that is.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Type
Main ingredient and pH
Curl and use
Take care
rows: Alkaline (cold) wave
Ammonium thioglycolate; alkaline, about pH 8 to 9.5. Works without heat.
A firm, long-lasting curl. Suits normal and resistant (hard to wave) hair.
Can be harsh on fine, tinted or porous hair; strong smell; can irritate skin.
Acid (acid-balanced) wave
Usually glyceryl monothioglycolate; a lower pH (roughly 4.5 to 7, as the maker states). Often used with gentle heat from a dryer, as the maker says.
A softer, more natural curl. Gentler on fragile, tinted or dry hair.
Can be more likely to cause a skin allergy; may give a looser result on resistant hair.
Thio-free (non-thio) wave
A different reducing agent, for example cysteamine.
For clients who cannot have a thio perm; results vary.
Follow the maker's instructions closely; not always as strong a curl.
Curl reformation (soft curl)
A thio rearranger or softener, then a booster and neutraliser.
Loosens very tight natural curl into a softer, defined curl.
Hair is dry afterwards; needs daily moisture. See the section on curl reformation.

blocks.note: The pH ranges above are typical. Makers differ, so always follow the instructions that come with the product you are using, and use the lotion and neutraliser from the same maker.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Do the consultation at the styling chair with the hair dry, in good light, before the client goes to the basin. You are deciding whether the perm can go ahead, how, and what the result will honestly be.

flow: Greet the client and read her record card
Ask about the result she wants and show her pictures
Ask about past services, allergies and health
Look at the scalp
Analyse the hair
Do the tests
Explain the plan, time and price
Agree and record

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: The curl she wants: tight or loose, how long she wants it to last, how she wears her hair
Decides the rod size and the wrap. Show pictures so you both mean the same thing.
Past chemical services: relaxer (which kind, and when), colour, bleach, henna, home dyes, earlier perms
Some cannot be mixed with a perm and can break the hair. Many Jamaican clients have used home kits, hydroxide relaxers or 'gradual' colour restorers.
Allergies or earlier reactions to hair products
A past reaction means no perm, or a skin test and a doctor's advice.
Health: pregnancy or breastfeeding, skin conditions, asthma, medicines
Check the maker's advice and ask her to check with her doctor when in doubt. Fumes can upset an asthmatic client.
How she looks after her hair at home, and how much time she has
A perm needs gentle care and moisture. If she will not do it, tell her the result will not last.
Her budget and how long the service takes
Agree before you start so there are no surprises.

blocks.h: Contra-indications: when you must not perm

blocks.p: A **contra-indication** is anything that means the service should not go ahead, or must be changed. Always look at the scalp first.

head: Finding
What you do
rows: Cuts, sores, scratches, sunburn, rashes or any broken skin on the scalp
Do not perm. Book her back when the scalp has healed. Lotion on broken skin burns and lets germs in.
A contagious condition (head lice, ringworm, impetigo)
Do not perm. Tell her privately and kindly, refer her to a doctor or pharmacist, and disinfect everything she touched.
A positive skin test (redness, swelling, itching, blisters)
Do not perm. Record it and refer her to a doctor.
A past reaction to perm or hair chemicals
Do not perm unless a doctor agrees.
Hair relaxed with a **hydroxide (lye or no-lye) relaxer**

Do not give a thio perm: the two chemicals do not work together and the hair can break or melt. Wait for the relaxed hair to grow out, or cut it off. A thio relaxer is a different case; follow the maker.
A positive incompatibility test (metallic dye, henna that contains metallic salts, colour restorers)
Do not perm. The hair can heat up, change colour or break.
Hair that is very weak, brittle, over-lightened or badly damaged
Do not perm. Advise conditioning treatments and a trim.
Recent bleach or lightening
Be very careful. Do a strand test and take advice from your instructor; most often the answer is to wait.
Hair that is too short to wind at least 1½ turns round the smallest rod
A perm is not suitable. Suggest another style.
Tight braids, tight cornrows or extensions in the hair; the client is unwell
Wait until the hair is free and the scalp is comfortable.

blocks.note: A perm over any chemical it does not suit can damage the hair for good. If you are unsure what is on the hair, do the incompatibility test and strand tests, and ask your instructor. Never guess.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Check
How
What it tells you for the perm
rows: Texture
Feel a single hair between finger and thumb: fine, medium or coarse.
Fine hair processes fast and breaks more easily; coarse hair processes more slowly.
Density
Part the hair in several places and see how much scalp shows.
Thick hair needs more rods and a longer wrap time; thin hair needs gentle tension.
Porosity
Slide your finger and thumb from the ends towards the scalp on a dry strand: rough is porous; watch how fast hair takes up water.
Porous hair takes in lotion fast, so it may need a milder lotion and shorter timing; very resistant hair may need a stronger lotion or longer timing.
Elasticity
Gently stretch one wet hair. It should stretch and spring back.
Poor elasticity (snaps, or stretches and stays stretched) means the hair is weak: do not perm, or take advice.
Length
Measure and look at the shortest and longest layers.
Decides the rod size, the wrap and the number of rods.
Condition and history
Look at the ends, shine and feel. Look at the previous services.
Tinted, relaxed, lightened or damaged hair needs a milder lotion or no perm at all.
Natural movement and growth direction
Look at the hair when it is dry.
Helps you place the rods so the curl falls naturally.

head: Hair
Usual choice
rows: Normal, healthy, untreated
Normal-strength lotion for normal hair
Resistant (low porosity, coarse, tight cuticle)
A stronger lotion made for resistant hair, or an alkaline wave
Porous, fine, tinted, highlighted or previously permed
A milder lotion made for tinted or porous hair, or an acid-balanced wave, with shorter checks
Very curly natural hair
A curl reformation system rather than an ordinary wave

blocks.note: Lotion strength names (normal, resistant, tinted) differ between makers. Follow the maker's chart for your product, and let the hair, not the packet, tell you if it needs a milder choice.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Test
What it checks
How and when
rows: Skin (patch) test
Whether the client's skin reacts to the product
Only where the maker asks for one
A small amount on clean skin (often behind the ear or inside the elbow), left uncovered
Usually done about 48 hours before (follow the maker's time)
Redness, swelling, itching or blisters: a positive result. No perm.
Incompatibility test
Whether chemicals already on the hair (metallic dyes, some henna, colour restorers) will react with perm products
Cut a few strands (with the client's permission) and test them with the product the maker's way
A reaction (fizzing, heat, a colour change or a strong smell) means no perm
Do it before every perm if you do not know the history
Pre-perm test curl
How the hair takes the lotion and how long it may need
Wind and process one or two rods on a small area before the full service, if the maker or the Centre asks for it
Do not process longer than the maker's time
Test curls during processing
When the curl is ready
Unwind a rod about 1½ turns and look for an 'S' shape. See the section on processing.

blocks.h: What you need on the trolley

head: Item
What it is for
rows: Perm rods and bands (several sizes)
Hair is wound round the rod to give the curl its shape. Plastic only.
End papers
Thin papers that hold the hair ends flat and smooth on the rod, so there are no bent 'fish hook' ends. Soak up some lotion.
Tail comb and wide-tooth comb
Tail comb for clean partings; wide-tooth comb to detangle (plastic).
Plastic sectioning clips
Hold back hair not being wound. No metal clips near lotion.
Waving lotion and neutraliser (same maker)
The two chemicals. Applicator bottles or plastic bowls with a brush.
Barrier cream, cotton wool or neck strips
Protect the hairline, ears and neck from lotion.
Gloves, apron, cape and towels
Protect you and the client.
Plastic cap, timer, record card
Keep in body heat when the maker says; time the service; record the result.
Spray bottle of water
Keeps the hair damp while you wrap.

blocks.p: The **diameter** of the rod decides the size of the curl. The hair takes the shape of whatever it is wound round.

head: Rod
Curl
Suits
rows: Small (thin)
Tight, small curls
Short hair; a very curly look; hair needs enough length to wind at least 1½ turns
Medium
Medium curls and waves
Most lengths; the most common choice
Large (thick)
Loose waves and body
Longer hair; a soft look; or large rods for volume and lift on short hair

ul: Rod sizes and colours differ between makers. Check the size on the rod, not the colour.
A section should be about as wide as the rod is long and no thicker than the rod's diameter. A section that is too thick will not process evenly.
Hair needs to wind round the rod at least **1½ to 2 turns**. A rod too big for short hair gives a bend, not a curl.
Using different sizes in one head is normal: smaller rods round the hairline and nape, larger on top, and so on, as the plan says.

blocks.note: End papers matter. If an end bends back on itself when you wind, you get a **fish hook**: a crimped, broken-looking end that will not go away. Cover the ends smoothly with the paper before you wind.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Method
How
Use
rows: Single (flat) end paper
One paper laid flat over the ends on top of the section.
Quick; fine for short or medium hair.
Double (book-fold) end paper
Two papers, one above and one below the ends, so the ends are held between them.
Longer or thicker hair; gives smoother ends.

sections.title: Preparing the client and winding the hair

flow: Ask her to remove earrings, necklaces and glasses
Gown her with a clean gown and a waterproof cape
Place a towel and neck strip round the neck
Shampoo gently with a clarifying or mild shampoo, as the maker says; do not rub or scratch the scalp
Towel-blot the hair so that it is damp, not dripping
Detangle with a wide-tooth comb from the ends
Put on your gloves and apron
Apply barrier cream round the hairline and ears; put a strip of cotton wool round the hairline

ul: **Shampoo gently.** Scratching or hard massage can scratch the scalp, and lotion on a scratch burns. Do not use a conditioning shampoo unless the maker says: it can coat the hair and slow the lotion.
**Damp, not wet.** Very wet hair dilutes the lotion; dry hair resists wrapping.
Keep the hair damp with the water spray as you wind.

blocks.p: Sections must be clean and even so every rod gets the same amount of hair. Use the tail comb for straight partings. Clip away the hair that is not being wound.

head: Wrap
How it is done
When you use it
rows: Basic (nine-section) wrap
The head is divided into nine panels: a centre panel with a panel on each side, and so on. Rods lie in straight rows inside each panel.
The usual pattern; all the same length of hair; simple and even.
Bricklay wrap
The rods are staggered like bricks in a wall, so the partings of one row do not line up with the next.
Stops visible splits between rows of curls, especially on short or medium hair and on the top.
Spiral wrap
The hair is wound down the rod in a spiral, not flat; the rod is held vertically.
Long hair; gives an even curl from root to ends.
Piggyback (double-rod) wrap
Two rods are used on one strand, one on the mid-lengths and one on the ends.
Long hair, when one rod would be too heavy or too long.
Directional or 'around the head'
The rods follow the direction the hair will fall.
A styled look with movement in one direction.

head: Placement
What it is
Effect
rows: On-base
The rod sits on its own section, at its base.
The most lift and root movement.
Half-base
The rod sits half off its section.
A little lift; a softer curl at the root.
Off-base
The rod sits fully off its section, below it, resting on the skin or the next section.
Little or no lift; the root stays flat; more movement at the ends.

flow: Part a section no wider than the rod is long, and comb it smooth
Hold it at the angle for the base control wanted
Place an end paper over the ends so that they lie flat
Hold the paper and hair between your fingers and wind the hair towards the scalp, keeping the ends flat on the rod
Wind with even, firm tension: no stretching, no slack
Fasten the band so that it lies across the rod and does not press into the hair or the scalp
Check there are no bent ends and that the rod sits in line with its row

ul: **Even tension** is firm without stretching. Too tight stretches the hair and can break it or cause pain and scalp damage; too loose gives a weak, uneven curl.
**Keep the band off the root.** A band that presses hard into the hair marks or breaks it along the band line (a dent in the curl).
Wind all rods in the same direction in a row, unless the style is directional.
Work calmly and keep the hair damp. If the hair dries while you wrap, re-wet it lightly.

blocks.note: If lotion is applied after the head is wound (the usual way), the order is: wind all the rods, protect the skin, apply the lotion to each rod, cover with a cap if the maker says, and start your timer. Some makers have a pre-wrap method where the lotion is applied before winding; follow the maker's instructions for your product.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Processing, test curls, rinsing and neutralising

flow: Check the gloves, towels, barrier cream and cotton wool
Apply the lotion evenly to every rod, soaking each wound section
Do not let lotion run onto the skin
Re-do the cotton wool if it is wet with lotion
Cover with a plastic cap if the maker says
Start the timer and note the time on the record card

ul: Use enough lotion to saturate each rod; a dry spot gives a straight spot.
Do not put the client under a dryer unless the maker says for that product. Heat speeds up the lotion and can over-process.
A plastic cap holds in body heat, which makes the lotion work, and stops it drying out. Use it only if the maker says.
Hot weather, a warm room and a hot scalp all make the lotion work faster than the packet says. Take the first test curl earlier on a hot day.

blocks.p: A **test curl** shows when the hair has taken the shape of the rod. It stops you under-processing (a weak curl) or over-processing (damaged hair).

flow: Start the checks at the time the maker says, not later
Put on gloves
Choose a rod in an area that processes fast (the crown or sides) and later one at the nape
Unwind the rod about 1½ turns without moving it off the scalp
Ease the hair gently towards the scalp with the rod still held
Look at the shape: a firm, even 'S' shape that matches the rod means the curl has formed
If it is ready, rinse the whole head at once. If not, rewind the rod gently and check again in a few minutes

ul: Check in **several areas**, because the hair at the crown, sides and nape may process at different rates.
A loose, flat 'S' or none means it needs more time. A tight, frizzy curl with no 'S' means over-processing: rinse at once.
Never go beyond the maker's maximum time. If the curl has not formed by then, rinse and tell your instructor; do not carry on.
Write the time and result on the record card.
Rinse the lotion out **with the rods still in**, thoroughly, with lukewarm water, for the time the maker says (often about 5 minutes). Aim the water so it does not run onto her face.
**Blot** the rods well with a towel. Extra water would dilute the neutraliser and stop it fixing the curl.
Take off the cotton wool and replace it with dry cotton wool, and re-apply barrier cream if it has worn off.

flow: Apply the neutraliser evenly to every rod, working through all the hair
Time it as the maker says (often about 5 to 10 minutes; some makers use two applications)
Gently remove the rods, without pulling the curl
Apply the rest of the neutraliser to the loose hair, if the maker says
Rinse thoroughly with lukewarm water
Apply a light conditioner or an acid rinse, as the maker says

ul: Neutraliser re-forms the bonds in the new shape. If you miss part of the head or rinse it off too soon, the curl will not last.
**Remove the rods gently.** The curl is still soft and can be pulled out of shape if you drag or stretch it.
Do not comb the hair roughly at this stage.
Detangle gently with a wide-tooth comb or fingers, from the ends.
Style by diffusing, air drying or setting loosely, without stretching the curl, as the client wants.
Check the whole head: the curl is even, no straight patches, no frizz or breaks, and the scalp is not red or sore.
Show the client in the mirror and ask whether she is happy.

head: Step
Typical time (follow the maker)
Who decides
rows: Skin test
About 48 hours before
The maker
Lotion on the head
Often 10 to 20 minutes, with test curls
The maker, then your test curls
Lotion rinse
About 5 minutes
The maker
Neutraliser
About 5 to 10 minutes
The maker
First shampoo after the perm
Often 48 hours later, or as the maker says
The maker

blocks.note: All these times are typical figures. They vary with the product, the hair and the weather. Use the maker's instructions for your product and the advice of your instructor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **curl reformation** (often called a soft curl or a curl relaxer-and-perm) is for very curly or coily natural hair. A normal perm would give a curl as tight as the natural one. Instead the natural curl is first loosened, then the hair is wound on rods and given a new, softer, defined curl.

head: Step
Product
What it does
rows: 1. Consult, skin and strand tests
None
Check there is no hydroxide relaxer and no metallic dye on the hair, and the scalp is healthy.
2. Apply the rearranger (softener)
A thio cream or lotion
Loosens the natural curl. Applied and timed as the maker says, away from the scalp skin.
3. Rinse the rearranger out
Water
Stops its action. Blot the hair.
4. Wind the hair on rods
Rods, end papers
Gives the shape of the new curl.
5. Apply the booster
A perm lotion
Puts the curl into the hair. Take test curls as for any perm.
6. Rinse and blot
Water
Rinse with the rods in, then blot.
7. Neutralise
Neutraliser
Fixes the new curl. Remove the rods gently.
8. Rinse, condition and style
Conditioner
Replace moisture. Style with a curl cream or gel.

ul: The hair is **much drier and more fragile** after a curl reformation. Natural coily hair is already dry and breaks at every bend, and now the chemicals have been added.
Do a strand test first. Never give a curl reformation on hair relaxed with a hydroxide relaxer.
Use only products from the same system, in the order the maker gives.
Moisturise **every day** with a leave-in curl moisturiser or a light cream.
Detangle with a wide-tooth comb or a pick, never a fine comb or a hard brush.
Wear a satin scarf or bonnet at night.
Deep condition every week or two; a protein treatment now and then if the hair feels soft and weak.
Wait the time the maker says before the first shampoo, and use a gentle, moisturising shampoo.
Avoid heavy grease, hot irons and tight styles.

head: Fault
Likely causes
Prevention or cure
rows: Weak curl, or curl that drops (under-processed)
Lotion too weak for resistant hair; too little lotion; too short a time; rods too large; hair too wet or dry; neutraliser diluted
Analyse the hair; choose the lotion and rods properly; use enough lotion; time with test curls; blot well before neutralising. A weak perm can sometimes be re-done later, as the instructor advises.
Frizzy, dry, weak or broken hair (over-processed)
Lotion too strong for porous, tinted or fine hair; left too long; heat or warm room; no test curls
Choose a milder lotion; start test curls on time; rinse at once. Treat with moisture and protein and a trim. Do not perm again.
Fish hooks (bent ends)
Ends not smoothed with an end paper; ends bent back as you wound
Use end papers; wind the ends smoothly. Cut off the bent ends.
Dents or breaks along the rod line
Band pressing into the hair
Fasten the band across the rod and off the hair; do not over-tighten.
Straight or uneven patches
Dry spots of lotion; sections too thick; uneven tension; missed neutraliser
Apply lotion evenly; thin even sections; even tension; neutralise every rod.
Scalp irritation or burns
Scratched scalp; lotion on the skin; allergic reaction; too long
Gentle shampoo; barrier cream and cotton wool; skin test; rinse at once and refer to a doctor if bad.
Hair lightened or changed colour
Lotion lifts some tint and colour
Warn the client; strand test on tinted hair.
A strong smell that lasts
Poor rinsing; too little neutraliser
Rinse thoroughly; neutralise for the full time.
Hair breaks off at the roots
Mixed products; incompatible chemical on the hair; over-processing
Do the incompatibility test; never mix makers; follow the timing. Refer to the instructor.

blocks.p: Give the client advice with the reason for each point. A perm that is looked after lasts months; one that is not looked after dries out in weeks.

ul: **Do not shampoo for the time the maker says** (often 48 hours). The bonds are still settling.
Use a mild, moisturising shampoo and a moisturising conditioner. Comb with a wide-tooth comb or pick, from the ends. Do not brush hard.
Avoid tight bands, bobby pins that pull, and hot flat irons. Little or no heat styling.
Rinse with fresh water after swimming, and wear a cap in the sea or a chlorinated pool.
Wear a satin scarf or bonnet at night, and protect the hair from strong sun.
Do not colour, bleach or relax over a perm without asking a stylist first.
Come back for a conditioning treatment, and book the next perm on the new growth when it is due.

blocks.note: Jamaica's sun, sea and humidity dry the hair and loosen the curl. Advise the client to cover the hair in strong sun and to rinse the sea water or chlorine out with fresh water.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Close and store all products in a cool, dry place, labelled
Throw away left-over lotion and neutraliser as the maker and Centre say; never back in the bottle
Bin the used cotton wool, end papers, neck strips and gloves
Wash, then disinfect and dry the rods, bowls, combs and clips
Put used towels and capes in the closed laundry bin
Wipe the surfaces and the trolley with disinfectant
Sweep up, mop spills and put a wet floor sign out
Wash your hands and record the stock used

head: Word
What it means
rows: Cleaning
Removing hair, dirt and product with detergent and water. It always comes first.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical that kills most harmful germs on clean tools and surfaces, for the contact time on the label.
Sterilising
Killing all germs and their spores, usually with an autoclave.

blocks.p: Write on the client's **record card** at every visit. The next stylist needs it to repeat a good result or avoid a problem, and it shows that the correct steps were followed if there is a complaint or a reaction.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, name, contact details
07/11/2026, Janelle Francis, Portmore
Hair and scalp analysis
Medium texture, medium density, normal porosity, good elasticity; scalp healthy
Past services and tests
Last colour 3 months ago (semi-permanent); skin test clear 48 hours before; incompatibility test negative
Lotion, neutraliser and maker
Normal-strength alkaline lotion; neutraliser from the same maker
Rods and wrap
Medium rods; basic wrap; end papers; off-base at the nape
Timings and test curls
Lotion on at 10:05; first test curl at 10:15; 'S' shape at 10:25; rinsed 10:26
Problems or reactions
None
Aftercare given and next visit
No shampoo for 48 hours; moisturising conditioner; trim in 6 weeks
Stylist and instructor check
A. Brown (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Client records are personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure: store cards in a locked drawer or a password-protected system, and never discuss a client's hair, health or tests with other clients.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can say why gloves, an apron, barrier cream, cotton wool and ventilation are used in a perm service.
I can give first aid for lotion or neutraliser in the eye and on the skin, and say when to stop the service.
I can store, handle and throw away perm products correctly and say why metal tools are not used.
I can explain the difference between hydrogen, salt and disulphide bonds.
I can explain a perm in two steps: reduction by the lotion, oxidation by the neutraliser.
I can compare alkaline, acid-balanced, thio-free and curl reformation products.
I can carry out a full consultation and say why each question matters.
I can list the contra-indications to a perm and say what I do about each.
I can check texture, density, porosity, elasticity, length and condition and choose a suitable lotion strength.
I can do and read the skin test, the incompatibility test and a pre-perm test curl.
I can choose rod sizes and say how rod size changes the curl.
I can section the hair and do a basic wrap, a bricklay wrap, a spiral wrap and a piggyback wrap.
I can wind a rod with an end paper, even tension and the band off the root, and explain on-base, half-base and off-base.
I can apply lotion, time the service and take test curls correctly.
I can rinse, blot, neutralise and remove the rods gently.
I can give a curl reformation and say why it is different from an ordinary perm.
I can name common perm faults, their causes and how to prevent them.
I can give aftercare advice with the reasons, and write a complete record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I blot the rods before neutralising so that extra water does not dilute the neutraliser.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Perm (permanent wave)
A chemical service that changes the shape of the hair by breaking and re-forming bonds inside it.
Cortex
The middle layer of the hair, made of keratin, where the bonds are.
Keratin
The protein the hair is mainly made of.
Disulphide bond
A strong bond between keratin chains that decides the shape of the hair; broken only by chemicals.
Hydrogen bond
A weak bond that breaks with water and heat and re-forms as the hair dries.
Waving lotion
The reducing product that breaks disulphide bonds so the hair can take the rod's shape.
Reduction
The chemical change in which the lotion breaks the bonds.
Neutraliser
The oxidising product that re-forms the bonds and fixes the new shape.
Oxidation
The chemical change in which the neutraliser re-forms the bonds.
Ammonium thioglycolate
The main ingredient of many alkaline (cold) waving lotions.
Acid (acid-balanced) wave
A gentler perm with a lower pH, giving a softer curl.
Curl reformation
A two-step perm for very curly natural hair: rearranger first, then wind and booster.
Rearranger (softener)
The first product in a curl reformation; loosens the natural curl.
Booster
The perm lotion used in a curl reformation to put the curl in.
Contra-indication
Anything that stops a service or means it must be changed.
Skin (patch) test
A small test on the skin to see whether the client reacts to a product.
Incompatibility test
A test on cut strands to see whether chemicals on the hair will react with perm products.
Test curl
A rod unwound to check how far the curl has formed.
Porosity
How easily the hair takes in and loses liquid.
Elasticity
How far a hair stretches and returns without breaking.
End paper
A thin paper that keeps the hair ends smooth on the rod.
Fish hook
A bent, crimped end caused by ends folded back on the rod.
Basic wrap
A wrap in nine panels, with the rods in straight rows.
Bricklay wrap
A wrap with staggered rods, so no splits show between rows.
Spiral wrap
A wrap in which the hair spirals down the rod; for long hair.
Piggyback wrap
A wrap using two rods on one strand.
On-base, half-base, off-base
Where the rod sits in relation to its section: most, some or least root lift.
Barrier cream
A cream put on the skin round the hairline to protect it from lotion.
Over-processing
Leaving the lotion on too long, so the hair is weak, frizzy and hard to comb.
Under-processing
Not leaving the lotion on long enough, so the curl is weak.
Cleaning
Removing dirt, hair and product with detergent and water.
Disinfecting
Killing most germs on clean tools and surfaces with a chemical.
Record card
The client's record of analysis, tests, products, timings, advice and any reactions.

c1.title: A consultation in Portmore
c1.text: Janelle Francis, 29, comes to a salon in Portmore for a perm with loose curls. Her hair is shoulder length, medium in texture, and stretches and springs back when a wet hair is pulled. She mentions that she has been using a 'gradual darkening' comb-through product from a shop to cover her grey for about a year. While parting her hair, trainee Orville sees a few scratched, scabbed areas at the crown where she says she scratched herself at the beach. The maker of the perm asks for a skin test 48 hours before the service.

c2.title: Winding practice at the Mandeville centre
c2.text: In the Centre's salon in Mandeville, trainee Kimberly is wrapping a practice head that has medium-length, healthy hair. She sections the nape with a tail comb and winds with medium rods and end papers. When her instructor checks the first row, some ends are bent and crimped, a few rods have bands that press into the hair, and the partings are uneven between rows, so splits show. Kimberly has also pulled the hair very tight at the front hairline because she wants the curl to last longer.

c3.title: Processing on a hot afternoon in May Pen
c3.text: At 2:00 p.m. in a salon in May Pen, trainee Leroy applies waving lotion to a client whose head is wound with 30 rods. The salon is very warm, there is no ceiling fan, and the maker says to start test curls after 15 minutes. At 15 minutes, a rod at the crown shows a loose, flat shape. Leroy decides to leave it longer, then notices that a rod at the nape forms a firm 'S' shape after only 16 minutes. The client says her ear stings a little. A cotton wool strip has been left soaked since the start.

c4.title: A soft curl for Natoya in Spanish Town
c4.text: Natoya Brown, 24, has natural, tightly coiled hair, down to her shoulders. She has never relaxed or coloured it. She asks for 'soft, bouncy curls' and says that her hair feels dry and breaks when she combs it. Her trainee stylist Delroy plans a curl reformation, using the maker's rearranger, rods, booster and neutraliser. He wants to rush the service because another client is waiting.

c5.title: End of day at the training salon in Kingston
c5.text: After a practical perm session in the Centre's training salon in Kingston, trainee Camille pours the left-over waving lotion back into its bottle to save it. She mixes a neutraliser from another maker with the lotion she has left, because the original neutraliser has run out. She stores all the bottles on a high shelf by a sunny window and puts the metal bowl used for the lotion straight into the dishwater with the combs.

questions.q: Janelle's comb-through 'gradual darkening' product worries Orville. Which test should he do before deciding about the perm?
o: A skin test, to see if her skin reacts to the colour
An incompatibility test on cut strands of her hair
An elasticity test, by stretching a wet strand
A porosity test, by sliding fingers up a dry strand
questions.why: Some colour restorers contain metallic salts, which can react with perm chemicals and heat up, discolour or break the hair. The incompatibility test on cut strands shows whether it is safe. The other tests check different things.

questions.q: What should Orville do about the scratched, scabbed areas at her crown?
o: Cover them with barrier cream and perm the rest of the head
Perm today but use a milder acid-balanced lotion
Do not perm, and book her back when the scalp has healed
Perm only the sections that are far from the scabs
questions.why: Lotion on broken skin can burn the scalp and let germs in. A perm must wait until the scalp is healed; barrier cream does not make broken skin safe, and a milder lotion is still a chemical.

questions.q: Why does the maker ask for the skin test about 48 hours before the service?
o: It gives the hair time to take up the colour restorer first
It lets a skin reaction show before the lotion goes on her head
It lets the stylist plan the rods and wrap for the whole head
It lets the test patch dry so it can be washed off safely
questions.why: A skin reaction can take a day or two to appear. Testing in advance shows whether the client reacts to the product, so a bad reaction is found on a small patch of skin and not on the whole scalp.

questions.q: Janelle's wet hair stretches and springs back well. What does this tell Orville?
o: Her hair is very porous and will take lotion too fast
Her hair is thick, so it needs a longer processing time
Her cuticle is lifted, so she needs a milder lotion
Her hair has good elasticity, so it is strong enough to perm
questions.why: Elasticity is how far a hair stretches and returns without breaking. Good elasticity shows the keratin is strong. It says nothing about thickness (density) or the cuticle (porosity).

questions.q: What most likely caused the bent, crimped ends on Kimberly's first row?
o: The lotion she used was too strong for medium hair
The rods were too small for the length of her hair
The ends were not smoothed with end papers as she wound
The hair was too wet when she began to wind
questions.why: Ends that fold back on the rod give fish hooks. An end paper holds the ends flat and smooth on the rod while you wind. No lotion has been applied yet at the wrapping stage.

questions.q: Kimberly's sections at the nape are about twice as thick as the rod. What is the likely result?
o: The hair in the middle of each section will process unevenly
The curl will be tighter, because more hair is on each rod
The lotion will run off the rods and onto the skin
The end papers will stay dry and the ends will not curl
questions.why: A section should be no thicker than the rod's diameter. Thick sections let lotion reach the outside hair but not the centre, so the curl is uneven and weak. Use thin, even sections.

questions.q: Splits show between the rows of curls on Kimberly's practice head. Which wrap would help stop this?
o: A bricklay wrap, with staggered rods
A basic wrap with larger rods in each row
A spiral wrap with the rods held upright
A piggyback wrap using two rods on each strand
questions.why: In a bricklay wrap the rods are staggered like bricks, so the partings of one row do not line up with the next and no splits show. Spiral and piggyback wraps are for long hair.

questions.q: Kimberly pulled the hair very tight at the front hairline so the curl would last. What is the right advice?
o: Keep it tight at the front, but loosen the hair on the crown
Wind with even, firm tension without stretching the hair
Use thicker sections at the front so the tension is shared
Leave the front rods loose and wind the others tighter
questions.why: Tension should be firm and even. Stretching the hair can break it and hurt the client; a tight wind does not make the curl last longer. The delicate front hairline is where over-tight winding does most damage.

questions.q: Leroy's first check at 15 minutes shows a loose, flat shape at the crown. What should he do?
o: Rinse the whole head, as the maker's time has been reached
Leave all the rods and check again in an hour
Rewind the rod, give a little more time and check again
Put the client under a hot dryer to finish faster
questions.why: A loose, flat shape means the curl is not formed. Rewind gently, wait a few minutes and check again, but never go past the maker's maximum time. A hot dryer would speed up the lotion and risk over-processing.

questions.q: A rod at the nape forms a firm 'S' after 16 minutes. What does this show?
o: That the hair at the nape has finished processing and the whole head must wait
That the nape is ready, and it is time to check other areas before rinsing
That the nape was wound too loosely, so all its rods need rewinding
That the lotion is the wrong strength for the whole head
questions.why: Different areas process at different rates, so test in several places. The firm 'S' shows that area is ready; if the others match, rinse the whole head at once so that the nape does not over-process.

questions.q: The client's ear stings and her cotton wool strip is soaked. What should Leroy do first?
o: Tell her stinging is normal and keep the timer going
Dab her ear with a towel and carry on as planned
Put fresh barrier cream over the wet cotton wool
Stop, remove the wet strip and rinse her skin
questions.why: Stinging means lotion is on her skin. Stop, remove the soaked cotton wool, rinse the area with clean, cool water and tell the instructor. If she is burning or the sting continues, rinse the lotion off the head. Do not tell her burning is normal.

questions.q: Why did the hot room make it more important for Leroy to start his test curls on time?
o: Warmth speeds up the lotion, so the hair can over-process early
Warmth slows the lotion, so he must leave it longer
Warmth makes the neutraliser stronger, so test curls are needed later
Warmth dries the hair, so the rods must be rewet before each check
questions.why: Heat from the room and the scalp makes the waving lotion work faster than the packet says. Starting test curls on time stops the hair from over-processing; the hotter the day, the earlier you check.

questions.q: Why does Natoya's hair need a curl reformation, not an ordinary perm?
o: An ordinary perm cannot be done on natural hair at all
An ordinary perm would make her curl even tighter
An ordinary perm would give only a little curl in coily hair
An ordinary perm would give a loose wave with no definition
questions.why: A normal perm gives a curl as tight as the rod, and very coily hair is already tightly curled. A curl reformation first loosens the natural curl with a rearranger, then sets a new, softer curl on rods.

questions.q: Delroy wants to rush. In a curl reformation, what is the correct order of products?
o: Booster, rearranger, rods, neutraliser, rinse
Rods, rearranger, neutraliser, booster, rinse
Rearranger, rinse, rods, booster, neutraliser
Neutraliser, rods, booster, rearranger, rinse
questions.why: The rearranger loosens the natural curl and is rinsed out. The hair is then wound on rods, the booster puts the curl in, and the neutraliser fixes it. Rushing or changing the order spoils the result and can damage the hair.

questions.q: Natoya says her hair feels dry and breaks when combed. What aftercare would help most after her curl reformation?
o: Daily moisturiser, a wide-tooth comb or pick and a satin bonnet
A strong clarifying shampoo every day to keep the curls clean
Brushing the curls daily with a fine-bristle brush to define them
A hot flat iron each week to keep the curl pattern even
questions.why: Hair that is already dry and fragile is drier still after chemicals, so it needs daily moisture, gentle detangling and night protection. Clarifying shampoo, hard brushing and hot irons all dry and break it.

questions.q: What is wrong with Camille pouring the left-over lotion back into its bottle?
o: It makes the bottle too full to close
It would contaminate the stock and change its strength
It breaks the maker's seal, which voids the guarantee
It makes the lotion thicker the next time it is used
questions.why: Used lotion has been in contact with hair and air, so it is contaminated and may have changed in strength. Left-over product is thrown away as the maker and the Centre say; it never goes back into the bottle.

questions.q: Camille mixed a neutraliser from a different maker with her lotion. What is the danger?
o: They may not work together, so the curl may not set or the hair may break
The mixture will smell stronger, but it will work just the same as a pair
The neutraliser will be weaker, so the curl will be looser but quite safe
This is allowed if the strengths printed on the two labels happen to match
questions.why: Lotion and neutraliser are made to work as a pair. Mixing makers can leave the bonds unfixed or damage the hair. Always use the lotion and neutraliser from the same maker.

questions.q: A client was relaxed with a hydroxide (lye) relaxer four months ago and now asks for a perm on the same hair. What should you do?
o: Give the perm, with a milder lotion and shorter timing
Do the perm but put the hair under a dryer to speed it up
Give the perm only if she has a clear skin test
Refuse the perm, as the two chemicals do not work together
questions.why: A thio perm over a hydroxide relaxer can break or melt the hair, because the chemicals do not suit each other. A mild lotion, a dryer or a clear skin test do not make it safe. Wait for the hair to grow out, or cut it off.

questions.q: A client's blow-dry went flat after she washed her hair, but her perm curl did not. Which explains this?
o: A blow-dry is held by weak hydrogen bonds, and water undoes them
A blow-dry is held by disulphide bonds, which water breaks
A perm is held by hydrogen bonds, which water cannot reach
A perm is held by salt bonds, which shampoo does not change
questions.why: Heat styles are held by weak hydrogen bonds, which break with water and re-form as the hair dries. A perm changes the strong disulphide bonds, which only chemicals break, so a shampoo does not undo it.

questions.q: A client has very short hair and wants tight curls. Her hair will wind only one turn round the smallest rod. What should you advise?
o: A perm using the smallest rod, with extra lotion to make up for it
A perm using a larger rod, to get a better wind on short hair
A perm with extra tension, to make the short hair reach round
A different style, as the hair is too short
questions.why: Hair needs at least 1½ turns round the rod to form a curl. One turn gives a bend, not a curl, and extra lotion or tension only risks damage. A different style suits her hair better.
